Teacher Resources: Start Here

This module is unpublished and only visible to course staff. It holds the teacher manual, syllabus, and setup notes for Digital Art Imaging 1, Semester 2 (Modules 17 to 32).

Course setup at a glance

  • Module format: every module is one week of work: Instructional Page, then NN.01 Mini Lesson, NN.02 Discussion, NN.03 Quiz, NN.04 Studio Project & Reflection. Quarter 3 = Modules 17–24 (Collage & Typography); Quarter 4 = Modules 25–32 (Drawing, Animation & Final Portfolio). Week 9 of each quarter is catch-up/flex.
  • Grading breakdown: Projects & Portfolio 60% · Classwork, Practice & Reflections 30% · Quizzes, Critiques & Discussions 10% (assignment group weights are already configured in this course).
  • Software: Pixlr E (free, browser-based), pixlr.com/e. No paid software required. Animation frames are drawn in Pixlr E and assembled into a GIF in a free browser tool, taught tool-agnostically.
  • Portfolio convention: students keep all work in a OneDrive folder named DigitalArt_Portfolio_LastName; Semester 2 files are named DAI_M##_<Item>_LastName with the module number (M17–M32).
  • Tier 3 project rubric (4 criteria): Understanding of the tools · Quality of choices · Craftsmanship · Intellectual honesty. Each graded studio project carries a native Canvas rubric scaled to its point value. The Module 24 Typography Project uses its own capstone rubric (Hierarchy, Font pairing, Alignment, Expressive type).
  • Two-module projects: the Surrealism Collage (Modules 19–20) and the Digital Mosaic (Modules 26–27) are graded once, on the final submission (20.04 and 27.04). The draft items (19.04 and 26.04) are 0-point completion checkpoints. The Animation Project is scored in both Module 29 and Module 30.

Files

  • Teacher Manual (PDF): full course orientation. Written before the Semester 2 module restructure, so it refers to Modules 3 and 4 by week; the content is the same.
  • Syllabus 2026–2027 (PDF): student and family-facing syllabus. Add your name, office hours, and email before sharing.

All auto-graded quizzes are multiple-choice or true/false with answer keys stored in the quiz itself. The Module 26.01 Mosaic History reading check is a completion-credit survey with short-answer prompts; skim, do not grade for accuracy.

assignments.title: Module 17.01 Mini Lesson: Masking in Pixlr E
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you build a full collage, practice the one skill that makes collage work: masking.

  1. Open pixlr.com/e. Create a new canvas.
  2. Bring in two images (your own photos, or provided practice images) as separate layers.
  3. Select the top layer. Add a layer mask and use it to hide part of that layer so the image underneath shows through.
  4. Change the top layer's blend mode (find this in the Layers panel, default is Normal) and try at least two options to see the effect.
  5. Take a screenshot of your Pixlr E workspace showing the Layers panel with your mask and blend mode visible.

Submit: Upload the screenshot.

Grading (completion):

  • Two images brought in as separate layers
  • A layer mask used to hide part of a layer
  • At least one non-Normal blend mode tried
  • Screenshot clearly shows the Layers panel

assignments.title: Module 17.04 Studio Project & Reflection: First Digital Collage
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Build your first full digital collage in Pixlr E.

Include all of these:

  1. At least three images (your own photos or provided practice images), each on its own layer.
  2. At least one layer mask used to blend or cut a layer into the composition.
  3. At least one blend mode other than Normal applied to a layer, chosen because of the effect it creates.
  4. A clear subject or idea: your collage should say something, even something simple, not just be images stacked at random.

Decide on purpose whether your seams will be smooth and hidden or visible and intentional, like the Dada artists you read about in this module. Either is correct as long as it is a choice, not an accident.

Reflection: In 3-4 sentences, answer: Which choice in your collage did you make on purpose (a layer, a mask, a blend mode, or how you treated the seams), and why? What is one thing you would change if you built it again? Type your reflection in the text box when you submit, or add it as a short Word document in the same submission.

Submit: Export as PNG. Upload here with your reflection and save a copy to your portfolio folder as DAI_M17_Collage_LastName.

assignments.title: Module 18.01 Mini Lesson: Three Balance Sketches
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

  1. Export all three as one image or three separate files.

assignments.title: Module 18.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Balance
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Revise your Module 17 collage, or build a new short composition in Pixlr E, to clearly demonstrate one balance type: symmetrical, asymmetrical, or radial.

Include:

assignments.title: Module 19.01 Mini Lesson: One-Sentence Concept
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you open Pixlr E, plan your Surrealism Collage.

  1. Write your concept as one sentence: "A ___ where a ___ should be" (or a similar impossible combination).
  2. List the images you will need (your own photos, provided practice images, or a mix).
  3. Note which balance type (symmetrical, asymmetrical, or radial) fits the mood you want.

Submit: Type your sentence, image list, and balance choice directly in the submission box.

Grading (completion):

  • One clear concept sentence
  • At least 3 images listed
  • A balance type named with a one-sentence reason

assignments.title: Module 19.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Surrealism Collage, Part 1 (Draft)
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Build a draft of your Surrealism Collage in Pixlr E: one clear, impossible combination built with intention and craft.

Include all of these:

  1. A clear Surrealist concept: one impossible or dreamlike combination (your one-sentence idea from this module's planning assignment).
  2. At least one layer mask used to blend your elements into the scene, whether your seams are smooth or deliberately visible.
  3. At least one blend mode other than Normal, chosen for its effect (matching light, adding glow, unifying color).
  4. A balance type (symmetrical, asymmetrical, or radial) applied on purpose to support the mood of your concept.

Submit: Export as PNG. Upload here and save a copy to your portfolio folder as DAI_M19_Surrealism_LastName. You will refine this piece in Module 20. The final version, your reflection, and the grade come in Module 20.

assignments.title: Module 20.01 Mini Lesson: Self-Critique Checklist
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Before you share your collage with a classmate, look at it yourself. Open your Module 19 Surrealism Collage file and answer each item honestly (2-3 sentences each is enough):

  1. Is my Surrealist concept clear at a glance?
  2. Do my masked edges look intentional?
  3. Does my blend mode help the elements feel like they belong together?
  4. Does my balance still hold up after all my edits?
  5. Is my file free of stray layers or unintentional gaps?
  6. What is the ONE change I am making this module based on this checklist?

Submit: Type your answers directly in the submission box.

Grading (completion):

  • All 6 items answered with a genuine 2-3 sentence response
  • One specific planned change named in item 6

assignments.title: Module 20.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Surrealism Collage (Final)
assignments.html:

assignments.title: Module 21.01 Mini Lesson: Type Scavenger Hunt
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Type is everywhere once you start looking for it.

  1. Find one serif typeface in the wild: a book cover, a sign, a menu, a website.
  2. Find one sans-serif typeface in the wild.
  3. Take a photo or screenshot of each.
  4. Label each image: name the category (serif or sans-serif) and point to one letter where you can see feet (serif) or their absence (sans-serif).

  • Correctly identifies one sans-serif example

assignments.title: Module 21.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Type Hierarchy Exercise
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Design a simple layout in Pixlr E that shows you understand hierarchy. Imagine you are announcing a school art event.

Include all of these:

  1. A headline (event name), largest and boldest text on the page.
  2. A subheading (date, time, or location), mid-sized, in a second color or weight.
  3. A body text block (2-3 sentences of details), smallest text, left-aligned for readability.
  4. Consistent spacing and alignment repeated across all three elements (rhythm).

Use one typeface family for all three, changing only size, weight, and color to build the hierarchy. Export as PNG.

Reflection: In 3-4 sentences, answer: Which choice did you make on purpose to build the hierarchy, and what would you change if you built this layout again? Type your reflection in the text box when you submit, or add it as a short Word document in the same submission.

assignments.title: Module 22.01 Mini Lesson: Mood Matching Warm-Up
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Letterforms carry mood before anyone reads the words. Practice spotting it.

  1. Open Pixlr E's Text tool and type the word "ARRIVE" three times on one canvas, once each in three very different fonts from the font dropdown (for example: one bold and blocky, one thin and elegant, one rounded and playful).
  2. Under each version, label the mood it creates and one real product, movie, or event that font style would suit (for example: a fitness brand, a romance novel, a birthday party invitation).
  3. Export as a PNG.

Submit: Upload the PNG.

Grading (completion):

  • Three visibly different font styles used for the same word
  • Each version labeled with a mood and a real-world fit
  • Exported and submitted as a PNG

assignments.title: Module 22.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Expressive Type Poster
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Design a short poster or ad in Pixlr E that pairs an expressive headline with a readable body font, then reflect on the choices you made.

Part A: The poster. Pick a real or invented event, product, or show to advertise. Include:

  1. A headline in a display (expressive) font chosen to match the mood of your subject.
  2. A supporting line (date, tagline, or location) in the same display font at a smaller size, or in a second complementary font.
  3. A body text block (2-3 sentences of details) in a plain, readable body font, left-aligned.
  4. At least one warp, rotation, or blend mode adjustment applied to a text layer for expressive effect.

Use no more than three fonts total. Export as a PNG.

Part B: The reflection. In 4-6 sentences, answer:

  • What mood were you going for, and which font did you choose for the headline to create it?
  • Why does your body font contrast with your headline font instead of matching it?
  • What is one choice you would revise if you built this again?

assignments.title: Module 23.01 Mini Lesson: Find Your Own Text-in-Art Example
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Charles Demuth is not the only artist to use letters or numbers as the main subject of a piece.

  1. Find one artwork, besides "I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold," where text or a number functions as a visual or compositional element, not just a caption or title. This can be a museum website, a book, or a search of a verified museum collection (a site ending in .edu, .org, or a named museum such as moma.org or metmuseum.org).
  2. Record the artist, title, and date.
  3. In 2-3 sentences, describe where the text or number sits in the composition and whether it reads more like a shape, a symbol, or a message.

Submit: A short text entry or a screenshot with your written description attached.

Grading (completion):

  • Names a specific artist, title, and date
  • Describes the text or number's role in the composition, not just that it exists
  • Source is a real, findable artwork

assignments.title: Module 23.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Text-in-Art Study
assignments.html:

assignments.title: Module 24.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Typography Project: Poster or Advertisement
assignments.html:

assignments.title: Module 25.01 Mini Lesson: Value Scale Warm-Up
assignments.html:

Before you shade a full drawing, practice controlling value on its own.

  1. In Pixlr E, create a new canvas at 1200 x 400 pixels.
  2. Use the Shape tool to draw six equal rectangles in a row.
  3. Fill the first rectangle white and the last rectangle black.
  4. Fill the four rectangles in between with a smooth progression from light to dark, using gray fills or brush strokes at different opacities so the row reads as one continuous scale.

assignments.title: Module 25.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Proportion & Form Drawing
assignments.html:

Draw one object or simple figure in Pixlr E that demonstrates both proportion and form.

  1. Set up three layers: Sketch, Line Art, Shading.

  3. On your Line Art layer, draw clean final lines over your guides.
  4. On your Shading layer, render your subject with a full value range: highlight, midtone, core shadow, reflected light, and a cast shadow.
  5. Flatten and export as PNG.

Reflection: In 3-4 sentences, answer: Which proportion guide or value zone did you place most carefully, and why? What one thing would you change to make your subject look more solid? Type your reflection in the text box when you submit, or add it as a short Word document in the same submission.

assignments.title: Module 26.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Digital Mosaic, Part 1 (Draft)
assignments.html:
Student-facing text:

Begin your digital mosaic in Pixlr E. Plan it and place at least half your tiles in this module. You will finish, reflect, and submit it for a grade in Module 27.

Steps:

  1. Choose a simple subject with clear, bold shapes (a face, an animal, a symbol, a landscape silhouette). Avoid subjects with fine detail; mosaics simplify.
  2. Choose your grid scale: coarse and abstract, or fine and closer to smooth.
  3. Build your mosaic using either the tile-by-tile method (Shape tool, one tessera at a time) or the grid-overlay method (pixelate/mosaic-style filter on a base image, then refine by hand with the Shape tool).
  4. Keep a visible seam or gap between tiles so the piece reads as a mosaic, not a blurry photo.
  5. Complete your plan and place at least half your tiles.

Before you draw a single frame, plan your animation.

assignments.title: Module 29.01 Mini Lesson: Storyboard Your Loop

  • Thin (vague description or missing reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 19.02 Discussion: Juxtaposition and Symbolism
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Look back at your one-sentence concept. In 4-6 sentences, explain how your collage uses juxtaposition (which unrelated things you are placing together) and symbolism (what at least one of those things stands for beyond itself, such as an idea, a fear, or a memory). Then compare it to the Fuseli painting The Nightmare or the vanitas still life on the lesson page: name one way your idea works like that example.

Then reply to one classmate: Does their combination feel impossible and dreamlike to you? Tell them what you think each element stands for, and ask whether that is what they intended.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (juxtaposition explained + symbolism explained + comparison to a named lesson example + reply) = full credit
  • Thin (vague, or missing the symbolism, the comparison, or the reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 20.02 Discussion: Collage Peer Critique
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your in-progress Surrealism Collage (screenshot or export). Then reply to one classmate's post with a real critique in three parts, 4-6 sentences total:

  1. What I see: describe their concept and composition specifically.
  2. What works: name one choice (a mask, a blend mode, a balance decision) that is doing real work, and say why.
  3. One question: ask about something unclear, or offer one specific idea for a stronger finish.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (own post + all 3 critique parts present and specific) = full credit
  • Thin (missing a part, or vague/generic comments like "cool" or "nice job") = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 21.02 Discussion: Reading the Rules
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Pick one everyday example of text design: a street sign, an app screen, a book cover, a poster. In 4-6 sentences, describe the hierarchy: what is the viewer meant to read first, second, and last, and how does size, weight, or spacing create that order? Name the alignment used (left, centered, right, or justified) and say whether you think it works.

Then reply to one classmate: Do you agree with their read of the hierarchy? Would you have arranged it differently?

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (specific example, hierarchy explained with a design term, alignment named, reply given) = full credit
  • Thin (vague or missing a term, or no reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 22.02 Discussion: Letters With a Mood
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Find one real movie title, book cover, or logo where the letterforms themselves (not just the color or an image) carry a mood. In 4-6 sentences, name what you found, describe the letterforms in design terms (weight, spacing, edges, curves), and explain the mood they create. Then say whether you think the designer paired that display font with a plainer font anywhere else on the same piece (a subtitle, a byline, fine print), and what that pairing does for the design.

Then reply to one classmate: Do you read the same mood from their example, or something different?

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (specific example, letterforms described in design terms, mood named, pairing addressed, reply given) = full credit
  • Thin (vague description, missing the pairing question, or no reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 23.02 Discussion: Reading Demuth's Figure 5
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Look again at how "I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold" is described in the lesson: a large gold numeral 5, repeated smaller in the background, surrounded by fragments of lettering and city shapes. In 4-6 sentences, explain what the numeral does compositionally (where your eye goes first and why) and connect it to the poem that inspired the painting, William Carlos Williams's "The Great Figure." Then say what you think the painting is really "about": a fire truck, a friend, a city moment, or something else, and why.

Then reply to one classmate: Do you read the painting's subject the same way? Point to a specific detail from their post that changes or confirms your own reading.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (compositional role explained, poem connection made, own reading given, reply given) = full credit
  • Thin (vague description, missing the poem connection, or no reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 24.02 Discussion: Typography Critique
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your poster or advertisement, in progress or finished, to this discussion. In 4 to 6 sentences, describe your own hierarchy, font pairing, and alignment choices, and name your one expressive touch.

Then reply to one classmate, using at least two specific typography terms from this module (hierarchy, alignment, font pairing, spacing, kerning, tracking, leading, or expressive type). Point to one thing that is working and one thing you would adjust. Be specific: "your headline is the largest element and reads first" is useful feedback; "looks good" is not.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (own choices explained with terms, reply uses at least two specific typography terms and names a concrete strength and a concrete suggestion) = full credit
  • Thin (vague description, generic reply, or missing a required term) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 25.02 Discussion: Spotting Proportion and Form
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Find one image (an illustration, character design, or photo of a sculpture) where proportion OR form is used especially well. Post it or link to it. In 4-6 sentences, name which one you are pointing out (proportion or form) and describe specifically what the artist did: where are the guide relationships correct, or where do you see the highlight, midtone, core shadow, and cast shadow.

Then reply to one classmate: Point out one value or proportion detail in their example they did not mention.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (image + correct concept named + specific detail + reply) = full credit
  • Thin (vague description, wrong concept, or no reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 26.02 Discussion: Choosing Your Mosaic Subject
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your planned mosaic subject and your grid scale choice (coarse/abstract like ancient mosaic, or fine/detailed). In 4-6 sentences, explain why that subject works for a tile-based image and why you chose that grid scale.

Then reply to one classmate: Suggest one specific way they could simplify their subject into clear color blocks (referencing the tile-by-tile or grid-overlay method from the lesson).

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (subject + grid choice explained + specific suggestion in reply) = full credit
  • Thin (vague plan or generic reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 27.02 Discussion: Mosaic Peer Critique
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your (near-)finished mosaic. Then find one classmate's post and give a full critique using all four steps: describe what you see, analyze how the elements work together, interpret the mood or idea, and judge whether it succeeds as a mosaic specifically (would it read clearly from a distance?). Write your critique in 4-6 sentences total, covering all four steps. Be specific and respectful; avoid "I like it" without reasoning.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (all four critique steps present, specific and respectful) = full credit
  • Thin (only 1-2 steps present, or vague) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 28.02 Discussion: Unity in Motion
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Find a short animation or GIF (from a website, app, or game). Link to it or describe it. In 4-6 sentences, identify one specific place where unity across frames is used well (the subject stays consistent while one detail moves) or one place where it breaks down (something shifts that should not have).

Then reply to one classmate: Add one additional observation about their example's timing or keyframes.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (specific example + unity correctly identified + reply) = full credit
  • Thin (vague example or missing reply) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 29.02 Discussion: Storyboard Check
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your storyboard (attach the file or a clear photo). In 4-6 sentences, name the action your loop shows, say how many frames you planned, and describe what changes between two of your boxes. Then explain one choice you made on purpose to keep the motion readable, such as the number of frames, the size of the change from box to box, or the delay you plan to use for every frame.

Then reply to one classmate: Looking only at their boxes, can you tell what action they are showing? Point to one box where the change from the box before it looks too big or too small, and say what you would adjust.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (storyboard posted + specific explanation of a readability choice + reply that names a specific box) = full credit
  • Thin (vague explanation, or reply that does not point to a specific box) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 30.02 Discussion: Animation Peer Critique
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your refined draft loop. If your Canvas discussion allows file attachments, attach your GIF; if not, attach a link to the file in your OneDrive portfolio folder (set to viewable) or attach one representative frame plus a one-sentence description of the motion.

Then reply to at least one classmate's post using this three-part critique protocol from the lesson:

  1. What works: name one specific effective moment (a smooth section, a clear idea, a strong pose).
  2. What's unclear: name one specific moment that reads as rough or confusing (a jump at the loop point, a size change, pacing that feels off).
  3. One suggestion: offer one concrete, doable fix tied to what you named in step 2.

Do not write general comments like "nice job" or "looks good." Every part of your reply must name something specific. Write your reply in 4-6 sentences total, covering all three protocol parts.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (own post + reply hits all 3 protocol parts with specific detail) = full credit
  • Thin (reply given but vague, missing a part, or not specific) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 31.02 Discussion: Choices You Can Defend
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post about the piece you are building for your final project. In 4-6 sentences, name your medium and at least two Elements of Art or Principles of Design you are featuring on purpose. For one of them, explain the choice, not just the label. "I used color" is a label. "I used a narrow, cool color palette so the piece would feel calm even though the subject is busy" is a choice explained. Finish by naming one decision in your piece that you are still unsure about.

Then reply to one classmate: Is their post a label or an explained choice? Tell them which, and suggest one detail that would make their explanation more specific.

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (medium named + two elements/principles + one explained choice + reply with a specific suggestion) = full credit
  • Thin (labels only, or reply is vague or missing) = partial
  • Missing = zero

discussions.title: Module 32.02 Discussion: Portfolio Showcase
discussions.html:
Prompt (specific, not open-ended):

Post your finished portfolio (attach the file or a shared link) along with 2-3 sentences on which piece you are most proud of and why.

Then reply to one classmate, in 2-3 sentences: Name one specific thing you noticed in their portfolio: growth from early work to later work, range across different media, or a caption that stood out to you as strong. Be specific about which piece and what you noticed; do not just say "great job."

Rubric (simple, 3-level):

  • Substantive (portfolio shared + specific pride statement + specific reply naming a piece) = full credit
  • Thin (portfolio shared but reply is vague or missing) = partial
  • Missing = zero
